title: You're Having My Baby

jokes.text: The newspaper being identified as the L.A. Times, not a tabloid, when Larry dismisses it as tabloid garbage
jokes.setup: Larry dismisses the pregnancy allegation story, saying 'these tabloids just make this stuff up'
jokes.punchline: Beverly corrects him: 'It's not a tabloid. It's the L.A. Times.'
jokes.explanation: Clean, efficient setup/punchline. Larry's defensive self-delusion is punctured immediately by a factual correction. Works because it establishes his character right away — he'd rather the accuser be discredited than face reality. Good economy, slightly familiar structure.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That's shelley long.

jokes.text: Larry reads 'Preparing to publicly allege' and asks: 'Well, if you're gonna cover your butt that much, why print it at all?'
jokes.setup: Larry is forced to acknowledge the article is in a credible paper and reads the careful legal hedging in the language
jokes.punchline: He pivots to attacking the journalistic cowardice of the hedged phrasing rather than denying the substance
jokes.explanation: Character-specific deflection: Larry can't attack the source, so he attacks the framing. Reveals his lawyerly instinct to find any crack rather than confront truth. Solid character comedy, not a huge laugh but true to his voice.

dialogue.speaker: Writer
dialogue.line: You know, I am prepared to publicly allege that Larry fondles my buttocks whenever I go in to pitch jokes.

jokes.text: 'She's a nut. Look at that picture. You can see the craziness in her eyes.' / 'That's Shelley Long.'
jokes.setup: Larry dismisses the Montana woman by pointing to her photo and claiming you can see madness in her eyes
jokes.punchline: It's not her photo at all — it's Shelley Long
jokes.explanation: Beautifully compact joke. The structure is perfect — Larry's confident wrongness is the comedy, and Shelley Long is a perfectly chosen target (former TV star, known for difficult reputation). Beverly's flat correction lands like a deadpan kill shot. Strong industry-insider flavor. One of the episode's early highlights.

dialogue.speaker: Other Writer
dialogue.line: Million, million and 5, depending upon if you can prove your buttocks is a source of income.

dialogue.speaker: First Writer
dialogue.line: Not since college.

jokes.text: Writer jokes about being willing to 'publicly allege' that Larry fondles her buttocks when she pitches jokes, asking how much she'd get
jokes.setup: The group is discussing the legal language 'publicly allege' and what it would take to make such a claim newsworthy
jokes.punchline: The female writer turns it into a hypothetical shakedown offer, treating Larry's potential scandal as a business opportunity
jokes.explanation: Edgy for the era, works as a send-up of Hollywood power dynamics. Mildly subversive but the joke doesn't quite land with full force because it's delivered in a breezy hypothetical register rather than with real satirical bite.

dialogue.speaker: Paula
dialogue.line: No. Baywatch was renewed.

jokes.text: 'Million, million and five, depending on whether you can prove your buttocks is a source of income.' / 'Not since college.'
jokes.setup: Male writer gives a mock legal valuation of the buttocks-fondling lawsuit
jokes.punchline: 'Not since college' — the female writer's deadpan confession that her buttocks WAS once a source of income
jokes.explanation: Three-word punchline doing enormous lifting. 'Not since college' implies a whole seedy biography with zero exposition. Perfect economy — probably the most words-to-laughs efficient joke in the episode. The setup's fake-legal precision makes the blunt personal admission hit harder.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, thanks for lying through your teeth. I appreciate it.

jokes.text: Larry walks in and asks if anyone saw the Montana article, gets flat denials, then: 'Well, thanks for lying through your teeth. I appreciate it.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks his staff if they saw the embarrassing article; they all claim ignorance
jokes.punchline: Larry acknowledges the obvious lie with sardonic gratitude, making the social performance of denial the joke
jokes.explanation: Very Larry Sanders — he knows the reality but accepts the polite fiction while making it clear he knows. The 'I appreciate it' cuts both ways: sincere and sarcastic simultaneously. Excellent character integration for a short beat.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: His name guy?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: No. He's just a guy.

jokes.text: 'Although I hope the thing about Baywatch is true.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just thanked his staff for lying about the scandal; Paula's only good news was that Baywatch was renewed
jokes.punchline: Larry's genuine investment in Baywatch being renewed, offered as a coda, reveals his shallow entertainment priorities
jokes.explanation: Elegant button on the scene. After the weighty scandal discussion, Larry's genuine hope about Baywatch deflates the drama perfectly. Shows his shallow vanity (Baywatch = beautiful people on TV) while being completely in character. Economy is excellent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I did not sleep with that woman from montana. No? No.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Just checking.

jokes.text: Artie asks to speak privately, the unnamed bystander is dismissed — 'His name Guy?' / 'No. He's just a guy.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks 'Guy, could you excuse us?' referring to an anonymous background staffer
jokes.punchline: Larry mishears 'guy' as a proper name; Artie's correction — 'No. He's just a guy' — is a miniature Abbott and Costello beat
jokes.explanation: Quick wordplay beat that works as a palate cleanser. Not a big laugh but it's clean and fast. Slightly undercuts the gravity of the scene in a pleasing way. Familiar structure limits originality.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Hey, I get some on a nightly basis. I'm still excited about mimi rogers.

jokes.text: Artie's 'No?' reaction beat after Larry denies sleeping with the Montana woman — a single word that says everything
jokes.setup: Larry passionately insists 'I did not sleep with that woman from Montana'
jokes.punchline: Artie simply says 'No?' — not as agreement but as a pointed, entirely skeptical one-word query. 'Just checking.'
jokes.explanation: This is Rip Torn's show. 'No?' followed by 'Just checking' is the platonic ideal of the Artie character — maximally skeptical, minimally sentimental, doing more with two words than most jokes do with twenty. The economy score is a 10 because it literally cannot be shorter. Character integration is near-perfect: only Artie has the authority and history with Larry to deliver this deadpan. A genuine 8+ moment.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, that would explain the lobster.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: How's that?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maine. Lobster.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I got it. You're working on a bit. I'll play along. Maine lobsters...

jokes.text: Larry claims he hasn't met anyone he likes in 6 months, then pivots to: 'Why do you think I'm so excited about Mimi Rogers?'
jokes.setup: Larry is defending his fidelity by noting his romantic drought
jokes.punchline: His excitement about a guest star reveals the pathetic thinness of his social life — celebrity proximity as his only romantic prospect
jokes.explanation: Good character insight packaged as a throwaway. Larry is excited about a guest star as a romantic prospect — a perfect distillation of his sad, show-business-blurred personal life. Character integration is high because it only works if you understand the Larry Sanders worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, that usually happens on Tuesday mornings, doesn't it? That's why it threw you.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Hey, I get some on a nightly basis. I'm still excited about Mimi Rogers.' / Larry: 'You get some WHAT on a nightly basis?' / Artie: 'Some of this, some of that. You don't wanna know.'
jokes.setup: Larry implies his excitement about Mimi Rogers comes from sexual deprivation
jokes.punchline: Artie claims nightly sexual success but deliberately obscures what 'some' means — the mystery is the joke, as is the image of elderly Artie as a secret sexual dynamo
jokes.explanation: Artie's mysterious virility is a running undercurrent throughout the series. 'Some of this, some of that' perfectly withholds information while implying everything. The 'Do you? No.' button is elegant. High character integration — Artie is the one character whose private life is both lurid and unknowable.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I once had a woman, and, uh... do we have time for this? I don't think we need to get into the details of this. She followed me across 7 states.

jokes.text: Artie enters grumbling about 'bags of crap' — Larry immediately: 'What, did Roseanne and Tom take your spot again?'
jokes.setup: Artie enters complaining generally
jokes.punchline: Larry's first assumption is that Roseanne (Arnold/Barr) and Tom Arnold have done something again — implying this is a known recurring problem
jokes.explanation: Good industry-insider joke. Roseanne and Tom Arnold were real tabloid chaos agents in this era; using them as the assumed culprits for parking-lot disruption is a sharp, grounded bit of showbiz satire. Works better the more you know the context.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Her name was Cindy halloran. Cindy halloran from pensacola, thank you very much.

jokes.text: Larry says he wants to handle the Montana story 'exactly the same way we handled the drunk-driving incident in '89' — Artie: 'OK. Gotcha.'
jokes.setup: Larry invokes a past scandal as a model for crisis management
jokes.punchline: The casualness of the agreement implies both men have a whole playbook of past disasters and a well-rehearsed system for burying them — neither needs to explain further
jokes.explanation: Superb implied backstory. The casual shorthand ('the drunk-driving incident in '89, OK?' / 'Gotcha.') suggests a whole iceberg of past catastrophes. It's worldbuilding comedy — the joke is what we DON'T hear. Rewatch bonus because the later revelation that 'we said nothing' makes the callback land twice.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: People are going to think I called her Cindy fuckpot or something. From the philadelphia fuckpots.

jokes.text: Larry compliments the tie; Artie explains it was 'given to me by the chamber of commerce of Pittsfield, Maine.' Larry: 'Oh, that would explain the lobster.' Artie: 'How's that?' Larry: 'Maine. Lobster.'
jokes.setup: Artie explains his unusual tie was a civic gift
jokes.punchline: Larry makes an obvious geographic inference and then has to laboriously explain it; Artie plays dumb, making Larry the one over-explaining a thin joke
jokes.explanation: The joke is more about the dynamic than the content — Artie letting Larry flounder while explaining a thin 'Maine/lobster' connection is nicely dry. The comedy is Larry's willingness to belabor a weak observation. Moderately effective.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: OK, I happened to say the word cum. So what? In front of Jessica tandy. Oh, that crybaby. She's heard all this shit before.

jokes.text: Artie: 'I got it. You're working on a bit. I'll play along. Maine lobsters...' — Artie playing 'straight man to a bit Larry isn't doing'
jokes.setup: Larry's Maine/lobster connection falls flat and he tries to explain it
jokes.punchline: Artie reframes Larry's awkward explanation as intentional bit-writing, refusing to let the social embarrassment exist — and then enthusiastically 'plays along' with a bit no one was pitching
jokes.explanation: Meta-aware moment — the show is aware that Larry Sanders the character makes bad jokes and sometimes his team has to cover for him. Artie's 'I'll play along' is both generous and faintly condescending. Good character texture.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, well, you don't become nude. He didn't take his clothes off. You become nude. I've heard that about you. No, I don't become... no. What you're thinking is that I'm very becoming nude.

jokes.text: Larry on air: 'The heap of garbage I'm referring to is the Los Angeles Times.' Audience cheers.
jokes.setup: Larry has been building to addressing the tabloid story
jokes.punchline: He calls the L.A. Times — the paper of record — a 'heap of garbage,' which echoes and inverts the episode's opening beat where Beverly corrected him that it was NOT a tabloid
jokes.explanation: Callback that gains resonance from knowing the opening scene — Larry is publicly doing the exact thing Beverly called him out on privately. The audience's cheering is in-world, which adds another layer: the audience doesn't know what we know.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Would you like a piece of gum?

dialogue.speaker: Mimi
dialogue.line: Oh, just half.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Do you wanna go out sometime?

jokes.text: Hank begins an audience anecdote about a woman who 'followed me across 7 states' — then trails off wondering if there's time, then names her: 'Cindy Halloran from Pensacola, thank you very much.'
jokes.setup: Hank pivots from the Montana story to his own stalker story as a parallel — starting to self-censor, then diving in anyway
jokes.punchline: He names her: 'Cindy Halloran from Pensacola' — turning what should have been a vague anecdote into a specific, legally actionable name-drop in front of a live audience
jokes.explanation: This is peak Hank Kingsley — he means to be helpful, creates a disaster, and does it with complete self-satisfaction. The hesitation ('do we have time for this? I don't think we need to get into the details') followed by the full name and city is perfect character comedy. Tambor's Hank would absolutely do this. The escalation to naming her is earned and the specificity ('Pensacola') makes it funnier. Strong 8+: the structure is nearly perfect and it only works because it's Hank.

dialogue.speaker: Mimi
dialogue.line: You don't waste any time.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Well, they're only on for 3½ minutes, so I thought I'd get right to it.

jokes.text: Artie furious backstage: 'People are going to think I called her Cindy Fuckpot or something.' Artie: 'From the Philadelphia Fuckpots.'
jokes.setup: Larry is mortified that his bleep will make viewers imagine a profane word where 'Halloran' was
jokes.punchline: Artie riffs 'From the Philadelphia Fuckpots' — treating an invented profane surname as if it were a real prominent family
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'From the Philadelphia Fuckpots' is constructed with the straight-faced cadence of a social register entry — as if the Fuckpots are a distinguished family. The joke works on the absurdist level (invented profane surname treated as real) and as character comedy (Artie's bone-dry delivery makes it funnier). The quotability is genuinely high — this is the kind of line people repeat. Justifies its 8+ score.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Boy, do I have a big surprise for you, Mr. Larry Sanders.

jokes.text: Larry revealing the 'drunk driving in '89' crisis plan was simply: say nothing. Artie making Larry reconstruct this slowly: 'I said... I said nothing. We didn't bring it up on the air.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie established earlier that they handled the drunk-driving incident a specific way
jokes.punchline: The plan turns out to be: do absolutely nothing. Artie makes Larry arrive at this himself through Socratic questioning, and the bathetic simplicity is the joke
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff is satisfying: Artie's entire crisis management philosophy is 'say nothing,' and the comedy is in making Larry realize this himself. It's also a meta-commentary on Hollywood PR. The Socratic structure (Artie prompting Larry to reconstruct it slowly) is the real joke — the dramatic buildup to a non-strategy. Strong 7.8.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Beth
dialogue.line: This is not my cousin. I'm Mary Beth nagler from montana. I'm having Larry's baby.

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'll apologize when we come back on the commercial.' Artie: 'I'm so sorry.' Hank: 'In 6 years, I've only been bleeped one time.' Artie: 'God, don't remind me.'
jokes.setup: Hank is defending himself after the Cindy Halloran disaster
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'God, don't remind me' implies the previous bleep incident was equally or more mortifying — setting up the next joke
jokes.explanation: Effective escalation setup. Artie's suppressed horror is funnier than anything explicit. Works as character comedy — Artie has clearly endured years of Hank-related trauma.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Gimme the button.

jokes.text: 'OK, I happened to say the word CUM. So what?' / Artie: 'In front of Jessica Tandy.' / Hank: 'Oh, that crybaby. She's heard all this shit before.'
jokes.setup: Hank's previous bleep incident turns out to involve saying 'cum' on air
jokes.punchline: The victim was beloved, elderly actress Jessica Tandy — and Hank's defense is that she's a 'crybaby' who's 'heard all this shit before'
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best joke. The escalation is perfect: we expected something bad, got 'cum,' which is already funny — and then the victim is Jessica Tandy, which recontextualizes everything (sweet, Oscar-winning elderly actress). But the real punchline is Hank's DEFENSE: 'that crybaby. She's heard all this shit before.' It's such complete, confident wrongness. It could only be Hank — there's no other character in television who would say this. Character integration is as close to a 10 as possible. Justifies the 8.6 craft / 9.0 impact scores easily.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Young lady, am I to understand you are blackmailing Mr. Sanders?

jokes.text: ON-AIR: Larry and Mimi Rogers' flirtatious wordplay — 'You become nude. I've heard that about you.' / 'No, what you're thinking is that I'm very becoming nude.'
jokes.setup: Discussion of nudity in movies
jokes.punchline: 'Very becoming nude' — a pun on 'becoming' (flattering) vs. 'becoming nude' (undressing)
jokes.explanation: Functional talk-show flirtatious banter. The wordplay works but is the kind of moderately clever double entendre you'd actually hear on a real late-night show — which is the point. Not a standout but serves the verisimilitude of the talk-show segments.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Move another inch toward Larry, and I'll take you down hard.

jokes.text: Hank offers Mimi Rogers a piece of gum between the jugglers and the interview — 'Oh, just half.'
jokes.setup: Hank makes small talk with a glamorous guest star in the most mundane way possible
jokes.punchline: Mimi Rogers' 'just half' — accepting gum at all, then specifying half, in the middle of a TV taping
jokes.explanation: The comedy is the mundanity. Hank offering gum backstage to Mimi Rogers during a taping, and her perfectly normal response, creates an absurdly domestic moment in a glamorous setting. Quietly funny.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Wonderful, Hank. Are you insane?

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Yes, I think I'm insane.

jokes.text: Mimi hesitates about dating because of 'this weird thing I read about in the paper.' Hank: 'Well, they're only on for 3½ minutes, so I thought I'd get right to it.'
jokes.setup: Mimi expresses reluctance to date given the scandal in the paper
jokes.punchline: Hank's explanation for his urgency is that the jugglers are only on for 3½ minutes — his entire romantic calculus is based on the show's running order
jokes.explanation: This is Hank at his funniest and most specific: his romantic window is defined by a juggler act's runtime. The joke captures everything about Hank — his entitlement, his obliviousness, his complete integration of showbiz logistics into personal life. '3½ minutes' as the justification for romantic urgency is the kind of hyper-specific detail that elevates a good joke to a great one. Justifies the 8.5 score — it's comparable to the 'never go with a hippie to a second location' anchor in specificity and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Is she the only one, or did you run across some muslim extremist who'd like to meet Larry?

jokes.text: Larry pitches dinner to Mimi Rogers: 'We could watch ourselves on TV.' / 'Watch ourselves on TV.' / 'We have a lot in common.'
jokes.setup: Larry tries to make watching themselves on TV sound romantic
jokes.punchline: He presents mutual narcissism as a relationship foundation — 'we have a lot in common' — with apparent sincerity
jokes.explanation: Excellent character comedy about Hollywood vanity. 'We have a lot in common' as a punchline to 'watching ourselves on TV' is Larry Sanders in one line — his entire romantic logic is narcissism dressed as connection. Mimi Rogers repeating 'watch ourselves on TV' in bemused echo makes it land harder.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Otherwise, you end up with, what we call in our business a crap column.

jokes.text: Larry: 'Come over to my house, we'll have dinner. Wanna do that? We could watch ourselves on TV.'
jokes.setup: Larry is pitching a date night to Mimi
jokes.punchline: 'We could watch ourselves on TV' — the ultimate narcissist's date activity, presented as a romantic selling point
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. 'We could watch ourselves on TV' is perfectly Larry — the pitch is both genuinely appealing to his ego and completely oblivious to how it sounds as a romantic gesture. Only this character in this world would say this, and mean it as an enticement.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I was, uh, personally abused as a child. No, not sexually. Physically. I was beaten, and I was kicked. You know, that sort of thing. Well, who do you think did it? The other kids, that's who.

jokes.text: Post-show: 'I thought Mimi was terrific.' / 'That will win the Nobel Prize for chemistry.' / 'I hope so. Don't forget to submit me.'
jokes.setup: Post-show debrief; Larry is excited about his chemistry with Mimi Rogers
jokes.punchline: Artie's 'Nobel Prize for chemistry' is a dry dig; Larry's earnest 'Don't forget to submit me' treats it as a real award he might receive
jokes.explanation: Sharp exchange. Artie's sarcasm is elegant and Larry's literal uptake ('Don't forget to submit me') reveals his self-absorption perfectly. The joke is that Larry cannot detect sarcasm when it's about himself.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What, you can't get pregnant from saying hello unless you say it to warren beatty.

jokes.text: Artie: 'She said she likes juggling. I like juggling. Sometimes the magic just appears.' / Larry: 'Well, you know, we are a variety show.'
jokes.setup: Hank is excited about his connection with Mimi Rogers
jokes.punchline: Larry's 'we are a variety show' is a deflating non-response that undercuts Hank's romantic fantasy with production-level pragmatism
jokes.explanation: Larry's response reduces Hank's romantic delusion to a production note. Hank thinking that both liking juggling is a romantic connection is the real joke — Larry's response just exposes the absurdity with minimal effort.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Me and Tom snyder... shoving match right there in the thrifty parking lot. You're right. You're right, that didn't happen. Roseanne didn't marry her assistant, either. She gets to make up this stuff. Why the hell can't I?

jokes.text: Hank: 'I'm always glad to meet a new twig from the Sanders family tree.'
jokes.setup: Hank introduces the 'cousin' with theatrical warmth
jokes.punchline: 'A new twig from the Sanders family tree' — an awkwardly botanical metaphor that sounds like something Hank rehearsed and is very proud of
jokes.explanation: Hank's self-satisfied folksy metaphor reads as something he thought of beforehand and is proud of — which makes it inadvertently sadder given the disaster he's about to unleash. Good character texture.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I'm on the one-phay.

jokes.text: Larry: 'This is not my cousin.' / Mary Beth: 'I'm Mary Beth Nagler from Montana. I'm having Larry's baby.'
jokes.setup: Hank has arranged a live surprise on air; Larry expects a real cousin
jokes.punchline: The 'cousin' is the Montana woman from the newspaper scandal — she announces her pregnancy on live TV
jokes.explanation: The episode's best structural payoff. The cold-open scandal, Hank's oblivious 'surprise,' and the live-TV setting all converge in one sentence. 'I'm Mary Beth Nagler from Montana. I'm having Larry's baby.' lands with maximum cringe impact because the show has carefully laid all the groundwork. The irony that Hank's attempt to be nice is what creates the disaster is perfect sitcom structure. High 8+ justification: structural payoff comparable to the best moments of the series.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Red wine gives me hives.

jokes.text: Hank's reaction beat after Mary Beth's announcement: 'Gimme the button.' — he asks to take back his promotional 'Hey Now' button he gave her
jokes.setup: Mary Beth has just publicly claimed to be pregnant with Larry's baby on live TV
jokes.punchline: Hank's first instinct is to reclaim his promotional button — petty, brand-protective, completely oblivious to the magnitude of what just happened
jokes.explanation: This is the best single joke in the episode. 'Gimme the button' is perfect in every dimension. Economy: two words. Character integration: only Hank's brain works this way — his 'Hey Now' brand is his most prized possession, and in the face of a live TV catastrophe, his instinct is to protect the merchandise. Originality: completely unexpected. Structure: the entire button setup (passing them out, giving one to the 'cousin') pays off in a callback that reduces a massive scandal to a petty property dispute. It becomes a cultural touchstone for the show. This is what a 9+ looks like.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I got a special thing for, uh, asian ladies.

jokes.text: After the big reveal: Hank takes back the 'Hey Now' button from Mary Beth.
jokes.setup: Hank has just introduced the Montana woman as Larry's cousin on live TV
jokes.punchline: His response to the disaster is to take back his promotional button — a perfect small gesture of self-interested deflection
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best comedic moment. Hank asking for the button back is perfect visual comedy that requires zero words. It encapsulates everything about Hank Kingsley: the obliviousness, the self-protection, the complete failure to understand the scale of what he's done, and the petty brand-consciousness. This is writing at the level of the Snip Snap anchor — total character revelation in one tiny action. A rewatch masterpiece.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: I got a special thing for, uh, asian ladies.

jokes.text: Artie, post-chaos: 'I'm so sorry, Larry.'
jokes.setup: The full Hank-caused disaster has just unfolded on live TV
jokes.punchline: Artie's flat apology — understated where it should be operatic — is the entire response to one of the biggest on-air disasters imaginable
jokes.explanation: Artie's flatness in a moment that calls for hysteria is exactly right. The comedy is in the gap between the enormity of the disaster and his measured, three-word response. Works as a perfect button on the scene.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Normally, you can only see to whitney houston's house, but it must be very clear tonight.

jokes.text: Artie to Mary Beth: 'Young lady, am I to understand you are blackmailing Mr. Sanders?' / Mary Beth: 'I just wanted to let you know in case you wanted to do something.' / Artie: 'Move another inch toward Larry, and I'll take you down hard.'
jokes.setup: Mary Beth reveals Hard Copy has offered her $5,000 for her story
jokes.punchline: Artie's threat — 'I'll take you down hard' — delivered with the calm menace of a much younger, more dangerous man
jokes.explanation: Rip Torn's Artie threatening physical violence against a pregnant woman with complete seriousness is the joke. 'I'll take you down hard' is delivered in the same register as 'good morning' — which makes it genuinely funny and slightly alarming. The character integration is exceptional: Artie is the one character you believe might actually follow through.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: If that's Kevin costner, make sure that we pretend we were just looking at the moon, OK?

jokes.text: Mary Beth, to Larry: 'Oh, I like the way you talked about us on the show. One day, I'll be able to show the baby that tape and say, "that's your daddy."'
jokes.setup: The scandal has just exploded on live TV and backstage
jokes.punchline: Mary Beth is obliviously heartwarming about the whole thing — treating a live-TV scandal as a treasured family memory
jokes.explanation: Dark and sad in the right way — Mary Beth's sincerity makes it more uncomfortable than if she were villainous. The image of a child watching a tape of their on-air parentage revelation as a keepsake is wonderfully awful.

dialogue.speaker: Mary Beth
dialogue.line: I loved you in star wars.

dialogue.speaker: Mimi
dialogue.line: Oh. I think you're confusing me with Carrie Fisher.

jokes.text: Larry to Artie: 'Is she the only one, or did you run across some Muslim extremist who'd like to meet Larry?'
jokes.setup: Larry is processing the fact that Hank let a stranger into the building and onto the live show
jokes.punchline: Larry catastrophizes — the logical endpoint of Hank's negligence would be letting in any dangerous stranger, and Larry jumps to 'Muslim extremist'
jokes.explanation: Dated and slightly sour. The 'Muslim extremist' joke feels like mid-90s lazy cultural shorthand for 'dangerous person' — it gets a pass as period-specific paranoia but doesn't have the sharpness of the episode's better comedy. The character anxiety is real but the execution is blunt.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So did I, by the way.

jokes.text: Hank calling the L.A. Times to defend Larry, ends up pitching the columnist on his own personal story: 'I was personally abused as a child... No, not sexually. Physically. I was beaten and I was kicked.'
jokes.setup: Hank calls the L.A. Times to defend Larry and deflect the story
jokes.punchline: He pivots from defending Larry to pitching his own abuse story as a more interesting column item — then has to specify 'not sexually, physically'
jokes.explanation: Hank's narcissism at full flower: he's ostensibly defending Larry but cannot resist making himself the story. The 'not sexually, physically' clarification is the escalation that makes it land — he's thought about this, he has a prepared statement, and it's pathetically weak. Only Hank would try to trade Larry's pregnancy scandal for his own mild childhood abuse claim. Strong 8+ justification.

dialogue.speaker: Lloyd
dialogue.line: She says, 'one large birthmark with 2 smaller ones above it at the base of the penis forming a mickey mouse head.'

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That is not my penis.

jokes.text: The lawyer Lloyd discussion: 'Michael Jackson wrote a check. Guilty.'
jokes.setup: Larry's lawyer suggests paying Mary Beth off might look like an admission of guilt
jokes.punchline: Artie's two-word verdict on the Michael Jackson settlement: 'Guilty.' — delivered as settled conventional wisdom
jokes.explanation: Maximally economic: three words summarize an entire cultural moment (the 1993 Jackson settlement). 'Guilty.' as a flat verdict delivered by Artie is both funny and a little devastating. High quotability because it works as a standalone comment on celebrity PR. Economy score near-perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Jesus, Larry, she knows all about little mickey.

jokes.text: Larry's Menendez Brothers moment: as Lloyd's questioning tightens, Larry says 'What am I? I feel like the Menendez brothers.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd is pressing Larry about what exactly happened with the Montana woman, and Larry starts to crack
jokes.punchline: Larry compares himself to the Menendez brothers — accused murderers — in the context of being asked follow-up questions about a parking lot encounter
jokes.explanation: Good period joke — the Menendez trial was a major cultural event in 1993-94, and Larry identifying with accused murderers because he's being asked uncomfortable questions is a nice deflation of his self-pity. Artie's reaction ('Ooh, what those boys did') is the real kicker.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No, she was one of the top people in the space program. Yeah, she was a waitress, Artie.

jokes.text: 'You can't get pregnant from saying hello — unless you say it to Warren Beatty.'
jokes.setup: Larry is admitting he may have said hello to the Montana woman
jokes.punchline: Artie's Warren Beatty exception — delivering a Hollywood-insider bon mot about the legendarily promiscuous actor
jokes.explanation: Elegant industry-insider joke with perfect structure. The 'unless' clause is the entire punchline — Artie's casual familiarity with the idea of Warren Beatty impregnating people through a greeting. Highly quotable. The joke ages somewhat but works as a period piece. Solid 7.7.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: She gave me a handjob in the parking lot at Denny's.

jokes.text: Larry's lawyer charges him $750, then: 'Make it an even 7. Don't tell anybody.'
jokes.setup: The lawyer announces his fee is $750
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately haggles him down to $700 and asks him to keep it quiet — suggesting he gets a discount from his own lawyer by being cheap and secretive about it
jokes.explanation: Small but revealing character beat. Larry's penny-pinching with his own lawyer — and asking for secrecy about the discount — says a lot about his contradictory values (he's famous but cheap). Good character texture without being a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: There's nothing wrong with a handjob, Larry. In my day, I've had plenty of 'em in far worse places than a parking lot. I remember one time I was visiting St. Patrick's cathedral. It was a Thursday. There weren't many people in the pews in the back.

jokes.text: Artie offers Larry lunch, basketball, shopping — Larry refuses each until: 'Buy yourself something extravagant? Cheer yourself up?' / 'Yep.'
jokes.setup: Artie tries to comfort Larry through various activities
jokes.punchline: Larry rejects all wholesome activities but immediately says yes to retail therapy — the reveal of his actual comfort mechanism
jokes.explanation: Clean beat. The list structure builds to the reveal of Larry's real preference — conspicuous consumption — which fits his vanity and insecurity perfectly. Not a standout but functional character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: There's nothing wrong with a handjob, Larry. In my day, I've had plenty of 'em in far worse places than a parking lot. I remember one time I was visiting St. Patrick's cathedral. It was a Thursday.

jokes.text: Larry claims he and Tom Snyder had a 'shoving match in the Thrifty parking lot' — then immediately: 'You're right. You're right, that didn't happen.'
jokes.setup: Larry is apparently ranting about others getting to make up stories
jokes.punchline: He invents a celebrity beef story, then self-corrects before anyone challenges him — revealing he was mid-fabrication when caught by his own conscience
jokes.explanation: Funny meta-joke about Larry's relationship with the truth. He invents a celebrity anecdote, gets caught by his own conscience, and admits it immediately while being annoyed that 'she gets to make up this stuff.' The 'Roseanne didn't marry her assistant, either' follow-up extends it nicely — he's mad about the double standard of celebrity truth-bending.

dialogue.line: I know the television industry has more than its share of pathetic types, but Kingsley has taken the prize.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Roseanne didn't marry her assistant, either. She gets to make up this stuff. Why the hell can't I?'
jokes.setup: Artie has just retracted his Tom Snyder story
jokes.punchline: He uses Roseanne's (real) tendency to exaggerate as moral justification for his fabrication
jokes.explanation: Good insider reference — Roseanne's tabloid persona was well-established. The logic (celebrity fabricates = I can fabricate) is funny in its twisted ethics. 'Why the hell can't I?' is a solid Artie button.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I didn't say anything about Denny's. I think you did.

dialogue.speaker: Lloyd
dialogue.line: No, I didn't, did I?

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Yeah, yeah. I heard Denny's.

jokes.text: Hank, mid-phone call, dismisses Artie with 'Am-scray. I'm on the one-phay.' (pig latin for 'phone')
jokes.setup: Hank is on the phone and Artie enters
jokes.punchline: Hank uses pig latin — 'am-scray' (scram) and 'one-phay' (phone) — as if it provides real conversational secrecy
jokes.explanation: Hank using pig latin in a professional setting is perfectly in character — he has the social intelligence of a golden retriever and the self-awareness to match. 'Am-scray' as a serious dismissal of Artie is quietly delightful.

dialogue.speaker: Cindy Halloran
dialogue.line: Hank, Cindy halloran from pensacola. I heard you mention me on the show.

jokes.text: Hank's list of personal revelations he's pitching the columnist: 'I'm afraid of the dark.' (pause) 'Yeah, I didn't think so.' / 'Red wine gives me hives.' / 'I got a special thing for Asian ladies.'
jokes.setup: Hank is trying to pitch personal stories to Howard Rosenberg as column material to replace the Larry story
jokes.punchline: Each revelation is more mundane/strange than the last — fear of dark, hives, specific racial preference — none of which are remotely newsworthy
jokes.explanation: Hank's delusional self-importance — believing any fact about himself is column-worthy — is fully expressed in this escalating list. The rhythm is perfect: each item gets slightly weirder, he assesses each one for viability, and the 'special thing for Asian ladies' is a perfect absurdist escalation. Strong character work — Hank thinks he's fascinating. This is Tambor at his best.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Call security. Call security now.

jokes.text: Larry and Mimi Rogers with a telescope — discovering it's Kevin Costner's house, then Larry can see 'to Whitney Houston's house' on a clear night
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to be romantic/impressive showing Mimi Rogers his telescope view
jokes.punchline: The impressive view turns out to be of celebrity neighbors' houses — Larry's romantic gesture is essentially celebrity voyeurism, and he has memorized whose house is whose
jokes.explanation: Good worldbuilding joke about the claustrophobic proximity of celebrity in the Hollywood Hills. Larry impressing a date by showing her another celebrity's house is a perfect encapsulation of show-business as a self-enclosed world.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: why don't I, uh... just come by, and we'll sit in the car, you know, and, uh... talk.

jokes.text: Larry to Mimi Rogers: 'If that's Kevin Costner, make sure we pretend we were just looking at the moon, OK?'
jokes.setup: The doorbell rings while Larry and Mimi are peering through the telescope at Kevin Costner's house
jokes.punchline: Larry's first instinct is to establish a cover story for their celebrity voyeurism — as if Kevin Costner has come to confront them
jokes.explanation: The plausibility of Kevin Costner just... showing up is zero, but Larry's social anxiety makes it real to him. 'Pretend we were just looking at the moon' as a cover story for telescope-based stalking of a neighbor is very funny.

jokes.text: Mary Beth appears at Larry's door — and Hank is also there, immediately fanboying over Mimi Rogers: 'Oh, my God. Mimi Rogers? I love you. I loved you in Star Wars.'
jokes.setup: The crisis arrives at Larry's home; Hank is already there for unclear reasons
jokes.punchline: Hank completely loses the thread of the crisis to gush about Mimi Rogers — and confuses her with Carrie Fisher
jokes.explanation: Hank mixing up Mimi Rogers with Carrie Fisher (and loving 'Star Wars') in the middle of a real crisis is quintessential Hank. The incongruity of his star-struck behavior given everything that's happening is perfectly observed.

jokes.text: Mimi Rogers correcting Hank: 'I think you're confusing me with Carrie Fisher.' / Hank: 'You are so great. You know, after I saw that movie, I started doing my hair in Princess Leia buns for months.' / Mimi: 'That's very flattering, thank you.' / Artie: 'So did I, by the way.'
jokes.setup: Hank is confusing Mimi Rogers with Carrie Fisher
jokes.punchline: Artie, deadpan, volunteers that he also wore Princess Leia buns — an image so absurd it operates on multiple levels
jokes.explanation: Artie's 'So did I, by the way' is the funniest line reading in the episode. The image of Rip Torn's weathered, grizzled Artie wearing Princess Leia buns is comedy gold — and he volunteers it without a trace of irony, as if it's simply a fact worth knowing. Perfect escalation: Hank's confusion is the setup, Artie's deadpan admission is the impossible-to-predict punchline. Character integration is essentially perfect — this specific absurdist non-sequitur only works coming from Artie. One of the strongest moments in the episode.

jokes.text: Mimi Rogers, meeting Mary Beth: 'Well, uh, congratulations, Larry.' — then she leaves
jokes.setup: Mary Beth shows up at Larry's home and announces herself as 'Larry's baby'
jokes.punchline: Mimi Rogers offers a perfectly calibrated social exit — 'Congratulations, Larry' — a polite, ambiguous phrase that communicates 'I'm leaving' without drama
jokes.explanation: One of the best reaction beats in the episode. 'Congratulations, Larry' does everything at once: it's simultaneously polite, devastating, ambiguous, and final. Mimi Rogers's graceful exit under terrible circumstances is funnier and sadder than any tirade would be. Economy score near-perfect — three words end a romantic subplot.

jokes.text: The lawyer reveals Mary Beth can describe 'distinguishing marks on your genital area': 'one large birthmark with two smaller ones above it at the base of the penis, forming a Mickey Mouse head.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd announces there are witnesses and damning details; Larry keeps denying everything
jokes.punchline: 'A Mickey Mouse head' — the specific, absurdly detailed, and somehow perfect description of the birthmark
jokes.explanation: The Mickey Mouse birthmark is one of the episode's great jokes. It's specific enough to be plausible, absurd enough to be funny, and Disney enough to be deeply wrong. The image of Mickey Mouse on Larry Sanders's genitalia is both an undeniable identify marker and an irresistible visual gag that the audience's imagination must construct. Larry's response — 'That is not my penis' — is perfect. High quotability; this is the kind of detail fans remember. Earns its 8+ clearly.

jokes.text: Larry: 'That is not my penis.' / Lloyd: 'I have to address every piece of information as it comes along.'
jokes.setup: The Mickey Mouse birthmark description has been read aloud
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat denial ('that is not my penis') treated with lawyerly impassivity by Lloyd: 'I have to address every piece of information as it comes along'
jokes.explanation: Lloyd's bureaucratic non-response to 'that is not my penis' is perfectly deadpan. The lawyerly phrase 'I have to address every piece of information as it comes along' applied to a penis description is delightfully inappropriate professionalism.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Jesus, Larry, she knows all about little Mickey.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are discussing the birthmark revelation
jokes.punchline: 'Little Mickey' — Artie's immediate adoption of an affectionate nickname for Larry's genital birthmark
jokes.explanation: This is the callback that elevates the birthmark joke to another level. 'Little Mickey' is an instant nickname that implies Artie is already familiar with this birthmark by name — which itself implies decades of locker-room proximity and baffling intimacy. The economy is near-perfect: two words do everything. High quotability — 'little Mickey' is exactly the kind of phrase people repeat. Strong 8.5 justification.

jokes.text: Larry's full confession: He met the Montana woman at a restaurant. She was a waitress. He met her in the parking lot. They sat in his car. 'She gave me a handjob in the parking lot at Denny's.'
jokes.setup: Larry has been claiming ignorance of the woman; Artie presses for the truth
jokes.punchline: The confession escalates from 'saw her in a restaurant' to 'she was a waitress' to 'she gave me a handjob in the parking lot at Denny's' — Denny's being the perfect detail
jokes.explanation: The best sustained revelation in the episode. The escalation is perfectly structured: each admission pulls the camera slightly wider on Larry's humiliation. 'She was a waitress' — worse. 'Parking lot' — worse. 'Denny's' — perfect. Denny's is doing incredible work as a setting: it's the most aggressively non-glamorous venue imaginable for a celebrity scandal. The structure earns a 9 because the pacing is precise. Character integration is a 9 because this is exactly the sad, lonely, furtive behavior that the entire show suggests Larry is capable of. Earned vs. cheap is high because nothing about this is random — it's the specific, believable, maximally pathetic truth.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Why didn't you tell me about this sooner?' / Larry: 'Because I hate myself.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks why Larry didn't come clean earlier
jokes.punchline: 'Because I hate myself.' — delivered as a complete, final, self-aware answer
jokes.explanation: Four words that encapsulate Larry Sanders's entire character. 'Because I hate myself' is simultaneously funny and genuinely sad — it's the most honest thing he says in the episode, delivered flat, as if it's just a practical explanation. The economy is a 10: there is no shorter or more complete answer possible. Character integration is as high as it gets — this line could be the series' thesis statement. Justifies the high scores because it transcends joke and becomes character truth.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Why didn't you tell me about this sooner?' / Larry: ''Cause I hate myself.'
jokes.setup: Artie asks why Larry didn't disclose the Denny's encounter earlier
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat, sincere 'Cause I hate myself' — not a joke, but delivered with the finality of one
jokes.explanation: Three words that land harder than most paragraphs. 'Cause I hate myself' works because it's genuinely true, delivered without self-pity as pure matter-of-fact Larry Sanders self-awareness. The comedy is in the directness — no joke, no deflection, just the bleak honest answer. This is peak Larry Sanders: the character comedy IS the drama. Highly quotable and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Artie: 'There's nothing wrong with a handjob, Larry. In my day, I've had plenty of them in far worse places than a parking lot. I remember one time I was visiting St. Patrick's Cathedral. It was a Thursday. There weren't many people in the pews in the back.'
jokes.setup: Larry is mortified about receiving a handjob at Denny's
jokes.punchline: Artie's attempt to normalize it by sharing a personal story — which casually reveals he received a handjob at St. Patrick's Cathedral on a Thursday, delivered with the matter-of-factness of a man sharing a nice restaurant recommendation
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's high-water mark for comedy craft. Artie's St. Patrick's Cathedral handjob story is structured with the detail and pacing of a master storyteller: 'It was a Thursday. There weren't many people in the pews in the back.' The specificity ('Thursday,' 'the pews in the back') makes it vivid and somehow authentic. The tone — equal to recommending a hotel — is the entire joke. Only Artie can deliver this: no other character has the moral authority (or complete moral indifference) to make this land. Character integration is a 10 because the joke literally cannot exist without the specific Artie voice. Compared to the anchor examples: this exceeds the 'Snip, snap' anchor in craft originality and is in the same conversation as the best jokes ever written for the show. A clear, justified 9.0.

jokes.text: Larry: 'That is the difference. You can get a handjob any day of the week. I get one, it ends up in the paper.' / Artie: 'Price of fame, my boy.'
jokes.setup: Artie has tried to normalize the handjob by sharing his own experiences
jokes.punchline: Larry's complaint that his handjob made the paper vs. Artie's freedom from press scrutiny, capped with Artie's world-weary 'Price of fame, my boy'
jokes.explanation: Good thematic button. 'Price of fame, my boy' is Artie at his most philosophically resigned — and the joke is that this is the actual lesson of the episode: fame turns ordinary parking-lot transactions into national scandals. The show-business satire earns its punch here.

jokes.text: The L.A. Times column about Hank's phone call: Hank 'babbling about hives, Tom Snyder, and a predilection for Asian women' — 'Kingsley has taken the prize' for pathetic types
jokes.setup: Hank's attempt to redirect Howard Rosenberg's column from Larry to himself
jokes.punchline: His 'revelations' (hives, Asian ladies) became a column item after all — just not the flattering kind. He is now the column's subject as an example of TV pathetic types.
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback. Hank's attempted fix becomes its own scandal — his 'revelations' are now in the paper exactly as he pitched them, but framed as evidence of his pathetic nature. The irony that Hank achieved his goal (column space) while achieving the opposite of his intention is a great structural payoff. 'Kingsley has taken the prize' is elegantly cutting.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Call the L.A. Times and get that punk on the phone.'
jokes.setup: Artie reads the column about Hank and is furious on Hank's behalf
jokes.punchline: 'Get that punk on the phone' — Artie's instinct is immediate escalation, calling a newspaper columnist a 'punk'
jokes.explanation: Short, sharp Artie beat. 'That punk' applied to a newspaper TV critic is perfectly Artie — he treats every adversary as a physical threat and speaks about a mild column as if it's a blood feud. Good character texture.

jokes.text: Hank's silent reaction beat upon seeing the column that's about him — assessing whether to put the paper back on Larry's desk or buy a new one
jokes.setup: Hank sees the column that humiliates him is in the paper Larry will soon read
jokes.punchline: His internal calculation: 'Should I buy Larry a new paper or just put this one back on his desk?' — the self-interested logic of covering up rather than confessing
jokes.explanation: Quiet, well-observed Hank beat. His cover-up calculation is completely transparent and doomed — he hasn't even figured out what cover-up to attempt. The mundane practicality ('buy a new paper or put this one back') is funny because it's such a small solution to a large problem.

jokes.text: 'She claims she gave you a handjob in a parking lot.' / Larry: 'That is so pathetic.' (long pause, everyone looks at him) 'Should've slapped her out of town on that one.'
jokes.setup: Lloyd reveals that as part of debunking her credibility, Mary Beth is now claiming the handjob story
jokes.punchline: Larry calls it 'pathetic' — then the room waits — then Artie says 'should've slapped her out of town on that one,' implying they all know it happened
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff of the Denny's confession is perfectly structured. Larry calling the true handjob story 'pathetic' is the peak of his self-deception — and the room's collective knowing silence is the punchline. Artie's 'should've slapped her out of town' is a great character button: he's both sympathetic and entirely pragmatic. The beat works because the audience knows the truth and Larry is performing ignorance.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Handjob in a parking lot at Denny's.' / Larry: 'I didn't say anything about Denny's.' / Artie: 'I think you did.' / Larry: 'No, I didn't, did I?' / Artie: 'Yeah, yeah. I heard Denny's.'
jokes.setup: The lawyer's summary mentions the handjob story; Artie adds 'at Denny's'
jokes.punchline: Larry catches that Denny's was never mentioned in the lawyer's version — then is gaslit by Artie, who insists he did say it
jokes.explanation: This is the second-best structured joke in the episode. Artie accidentally reveals he knows about Denny's (which Larry only told him privately), then confidently gaslights Larry — 'Yeah, yeah, I heard Denny's' — to avoid admitting he betrayed the confidence to Lloyd. The structure is airtight: setup (Denny's reference), complication (Larry notices), punchline (Artie's shameless insistence). Only Artie has the authority and composure to gaslight his own boss. The gaslighting is both funny and a little sinister — which is exactly right for Artie. Earns its 8.7 clearly.

jokes.text: Hank's office: Three women waiting — Kim Fugiwa, Jennifer Chen, and 'Cindy Halloran from Pensacola. I heard you mention me on the show.'
jokes.setup: The episode has been building multiple of Hank's disasters simultaneously
jokes.punchline: Cindy Halloran — the woman Hank named on live TV — has shown up in person, having traveled to the studio after hearing her name on air
jokes.explanation: The Cindy Halloran callback is a beautiful structural payoff. Hank named her on live TV; now she's arrived. The fact that two Asian women are also waiting (presumably connected to Hank's 'special thing for Asian ladies' pitch) adds an extra layer of karmic horror. Hank's cheery 'Well, you look great!' followed immediately by 'Call security' is a perfect character beat.

jokes.text: Hank sees Cindy Halloran, says 'You look great!', then immediately to his assistant: 'Call security. Call security now.'
jokes.setup: Cindy Halloran has arrived at the studio after being named on air
jokes.punchline: Hank maintains social pleasantries ('You look great!') and simultaneously calls for emergency security — the gap between performed warmth and panicked reality is the joke
jokes.explanation: Hank's social performance collapsing in real time. 'You look great!' and 'Call security now' delivered in immediate succession shows Hank cannot stop being a glad-handing entertainer even when facing a genuine security threat. The beat is tight, character-specific, and very funny. High character integration.

jokes.text: Hank to the two Asian women in his waiting area: 'Kon'nichi wa.'
jokes.setup: Kim Fugiwa and Jennifer Chen are waiting in Hank's office; we know from the phone call that Hank has a 'special thing for Asian ladies'
jokes.punchline: Hank greets them in Japanese — awkward, probably wrong (one may not be Japanese), and cringe-makingly enthusiastic given what we know about his 'thing'
jokes.explanation: The callback payoff of the Asian ladies joke is beautifully handled. One word — 'Kon'nichi wa' — does all the work. Hank's eager greeting, combined with what we know about his 'special thing,' makes it simultaneously funny and deeply uncomfortable. The economy is near-perfect. Strong callback payoff.

jokes.text: Hank to Mimi Rogers (playing show business host to the end): 'Oh, you were terrific on the show, by the way. We just absolutely loved it, yeah. You've gotta come back again sometime.'
jokes.setup: Hank is in the middle of a crisis involving three waiting women and a stalker in his office
jokes.punchline: He seamlessly pivots to professional pleasantries with Mimi Rogers as if nothing is happening
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Hank's instinct to perform showbiz warmth even mid-crisis is very Hank. Not the strongest joke but consistent character work.

jokes.text: Larry calls Mimi to try to revive the date: '...that problem has been taken care of. Uh-huh. Yeah. No, I understand, but... All right, look, why don't I, uh... just come by, and we'll sit in the car, you know, and, uh... talk.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to recover the Mimi Rogers date situation after Mary Beth's ambush
jokes.punchline: 'We'll sit in the car... talk' — directly echoing the exact description of what happened with Mary Beth at Denny's, framed as a romantic overture
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and its finest structural achievement. Everything in the episode — the Montana story, the Denny's confession, the handjob, the attempts to manage Larry's image — collapses into a single, perfect final beat: Larry proposing to Mimi Rogers exactly the same situation that created the scandal in the first place. 'We'll sit in the car... talk' is a pitch-perfect callback that works as comedy, character revelation, and thematic statement simultaneously. Larry has learned absolutely nothing. This is the show at the level of the great sitcom closers — earned, specific, and devastating in its clarity about who Larry Sanders is. Exceeds the 8.0 anchor. Comparable to the Snip Snap caliber in its multi-layered payoff.

jokes.text: Larry's final call to Mimi Rogers: '...just come by, and we'll sit in the car, you know, and, uh... talk.'
jokes.setup: Larry is trying to salvage his date with Mimi Rogers after the Mary Beth disaster
jokes.punchline: He proposes they 'sit in the car' — an exact echo of how the Denny's parking-lot encounter began. He's pitching the same scenario that created this entire crisis.
jokes.explanation: The episode's closing joke and one of its finest structural achievements. Larry has learned nothing. His closing pitch to Mimi Rogers is identical to the behavior that started the whole catastrophe — 'sit in the car... talk.' The pause before 'talk' is perfect. The episode ends on the joke that is the entire show: Larry's compulsive self-sabotage is irrepressible. This earns high scores because the callback is deliberate, the irony is rich, and it's a complete thematic statement in six words. The beat before 'talk' is an implied awkward silence that's the real punchline.

tmdb_overview: Larry's chances with Mimi Rogers drop dramatically when a woman from Montana turns up with the claim that she's carrying Larry's baby.
